questions.question: What distinguishes a quantum network from quantum processors connected only through ordinary cloud APIs?
options: Its nodes can exchange qubits or distribute entangled states over quantum channels
Its classical API uses lower latency JSON
Every processor is made by the same vendor
It always runs a quantum key distribution protocol
questions.explanation: Classical orchestration around quantum devices is useful, but a quantum network requires a quantum data path that exchanges qubits or establishes entanglement.

questions.question: Why can a quantum repeater not regenerate a signal by copying it like a classical repeater?
options: The no-cloning theorem forbids perfect copying of an unknown quantum state
Quantum links have no measurable loss
Classical messages cannot cross a quantum node
Bell pairs have infinite lifetime
questions.explanation: A repeater must use protocols such as heralded link generation and entanglement swapping because it cannot inspect and perfectly copy an arbitrary unknown state.

questions.question: A three-link route buffers successful elementary pairs while the slowest link retries. What new risk does buffering introduce?
options: The oldest stored pair can decohere before swapping finishes
The no-cloning theorem stops applying
Every link becomes deterministic
Classical authentication is no longer required
questions.explanation: Buffering can improve yield, but it turns quantum-memory lifetime and pair age into route constraints.

questions.question: What is the main trade-off of an entanglement purification round?
options: It can improve fidelity by consuming multiple pairs and sometimes producing no output pair
It copies one Bell pair into two perfect pairs
It removes every classical round trip
It guarantees a higher delivery rate
questions.explanation: Purification or distillation spends pair yield, memory, operations, and signalling to probabilistically improve quality.

questions.question: Which set of fields best describes an application-level entanglement service contract?
options: Endpoints, pair count, minimum fidelity, rate or deadline, synchronization, and trust requirements
Only physical distance in kilometers
Only the IP address of one detector
A promise that every attempt will succeed
questions.explanation: Routing and admission need a multidimensional contract because quality, scarcity, time, and trust can fail independently.

questions.question: A delayed herald carries a valid controller signature but belongs to an expired reservation. Which control is missing?
options: Freshness and replay binding to the current request, sequence, and expiry
A second copy of the quantum state
A longer CSS animation
A route with no classical network
questions.explanation: Authentication proves who signed a message, not that the message is current. Pair-granularity control evidence also needs correlation and freshness.

questions.question: Why can a physically connected shortest path still be the wrong route?
options: It may lack memory, pair capacity, fidelity, generation rate, deadline headroom, or an acceptable trust boundary
Quantum routes must always use the most repeaters
Distance never affects photon loss
Only classical bandwidth matters
questions.explanation: Quantum routing must account for scarce, expiring, probabilistic resources rather than topology alone.

questions.question: What is the most defensible use of a quantum-network simulator?
options: Compare protocols and narrow experiments using explicit calibrated assumptions
Prove that unmodeled hardware will behave identically
Replace all testbed measurements
Claim production readiness from one favorable run
questions.explanation: Discrete-event simulation is valuable for protocol and resource studies, but its conclusions remain conditional on hardware, noise, scheduling, and workload models.
